prompt: The budget `shop-monthly` reaches 100% of its 50 dollars on the 25th. What happens to the machines that are spending?
hint: A budget with only notifications.

choices.text: AWS stops them, and starts them again on the 1st
choices.why: Nothing in a budget with only notifications touches a resource. That belief is how bills grow past the number.

choices.text: They keep running, and AWS refuses to bill past 50 dollars
choices.why: The budget is not a ceiling on the bill. Every hour after the 25th is charged like every hour before it.

choices.text: They keep running and charging; the subscribers are told
choices.why: Right. A notification informs somebody, and somebody has to act. Even a budget action only applies a policy or stops named instances.

choices.text: New machines are refused, and the running ones carry on
choices.why: That is what a budget ACTION with a deny policy would do, if one had been configured. A notification refuses nothing.

prompt: On the 4th of the month, with 6 of the 50 dollars spent, `aws+billing@example.com` receives an alert from `shop-monthly`. Which notification sent it?
hint: 6 dollars is 12% of the budget.

choices.text: The actual one at 80%, because the forecast needs a month of history first
choices.why: Actual compares what was spent, 12% here, against 80%. It cannot fire at 12%.

choices.text: The forecasted one at 100%: the month is projected to end over 50
choices.why: Right. The rate of spending changed, and the projection for the month's end passed 50 dollars. It is the early warning.

choices.text: Neither: a budget sends nothing until the period has closed and the bill is issued
choices.why: Budgets are checked during the period, at each refresh, which is the point of having them.

choices.text: The SNS topic, which tells every subscriber on each refresh
choices.why: The topic is a subscriber of the forecasted notification, not a notification of its own. It only hears what that notification sends.

prompt: A new account runs on promotional credits. Its cost budget, created with the defaults, has shown almost nothing for three months. What is the risk?
hint: Read `CostTypes` in the transcript.

choices.text: None: credits are not money, so the usage they cover is not cost
choices.why: The usage is real and has a price; the credits pay it for now. When they end, the same usage is paid with the card.

choices.text: The budget is broken, because a budget cannot watch an account with credits
choices.why: It works as told: with `IncludeCredit` true it subtracts the credits, so it reports what is charged after them.

choices.text: Credits are subtracted by default, so the usage stays hidden until they run out
choices.why: Right. `IncludeCredit: true` nets the credits out. A budget with it set to false watches the usage itself, and shows the month that is coming.

choices.text: The forecast is wrong, since it never has five weeks of real history
choices.why: Three months is more than five weeks. The forecast is of the net cost, which is the budget's setting, not a lack of history.

prompt: Which of these can a budget ACTION do when its threshold is crossed, according to AWS's documentation? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three kinds, and none of them removes anything.

choices.text: Attach an IAM policy to a role, such as one denying new instances
choices.why: Right. The policy is applied by the role you give the budget, and the running instances are untouched.

choices.text: Delete the volumes of the instances that caused the cost
choices.why: No budget action deletes. Deleting is the one thing that ends a resource's cost, and it stays a person's decision.

choices.text: Apply an SCP to an organisational unit, from the management account
choices.why: Right. Only the management account attaches SCPs, so only its budgets can take this action.

choices.text: Stop named EC2 instances
choices.why: Right. Through Systems Manager. A stopped instance's disks still charge for what they hold.

choices.text: Raise the budget's own limit so the alert stops repeating
choices.why: A budget does not edit itself. Changing the number is `update-budget`, done by somebody.

prompt: `shop-monthly` is 50 dollars a month with an actual notification at 80%. At how many dollars of actual cost does it fire?
hint: 80% of the limit.

prompt: In the lab, `describe-subscribers-for-notification` answers with a server error. What may you conclude about the SNS subscriber in `notifications.json`?
hint: A 500 is about moto, not about your file.

choices.text: Nothing either way: moto cannot show its subscribers
choices.why: Right. `create-budget` accepted the file, and the operation that would read the subscribers back is missing from moto.

choices.text: That the topic was refused, so the alert will reach only the mailbox
choices.why: A refusal would have failed `create-budget`, which printed nothing and succeeded. The 500 came from a different operation.

choices.text: That the topic needs a policy allowing `budgets.amazonaws.com` to publish
choices.why: True of AWS, and the section says so, but moto does not judge topic policies; the error says nothing about one.

choices.text: That SNS subscribers are allowed only on actual notifications
choices.why: Either kind of notification may tell a topic; the shop's forecasted one does.

prompt: `get-resources` with no filter printed the bucket `shop-assets` and one instance. The bucket `shop-logs` and a `t3.medium` also exist. Why are they missing?
hint: What does that API list?

choices.text: moto forgets resources created without a region
choices.why: Both were created in `sa-east-1`, and `describe-instances` still lists the `t3.medium`.

choices.text: The API lists only resources that carry tags or once did
choices.why: Right. A resource never tagged is invisible to it, so the untagged ones have to be found by asking each service.

choices.text: A query with no filter returns only the first page of results
choices.why: Two resources are far from a page. The answer is complete for what the API covers.

choices.text: Tag policies hide resources that do not comply with them
choices.why: No tag policy existed yet at that point, and a policy never hides a resource from a listing.

prompt: The shop wants AWS to refuse any instance launched without a `team` tag. Which tool does that?
hint: One tool fixes the spelling; another refuses the request.

choices.text: A tag policy with `enforced_for` naming `ec2:instance`
choices.why: That refuses a wrong value or spelling. A resource with no tags at all is not reported as non-compliant, so it passes.

choices.text: Activating `team` as a cost allocation tag in Billing
choices.why: Activation decides which keys split the bill. It refuses no request and requires no tag.

choices.text: An SCP denying `ec2:RunInstances` when `aws:RequestTag/team` is absent
choices.why: Right. The condition looks at the tags in the request itself, and the deny refuses a launch that carries none; lesson 4 writes SCPs.

choices.text: A budget filtered by the tag `team`, with an action at 100%
choices.why: A budget watches cost after it happens, and its action would come after the spending. It never sees a launch request.

prompt: In the lab, an instance tagged `team=marketing` starts although the attached tag policy allows only web, data and finance. What does that show?
hint: Who stored the policy, and who judged it?

choices.text: That `enforced_for` covers only instances created after the policy
choices.why: This instance was created after the policy was attached, and it was still accepted.

choices.text: That moto stores tag policies and does not enforce them
choices.why: Right. moto kept and attached the policy and judged nothing. AWS refuses that value in an account the policy covers.

choices.text: That tag policies apply to buckets and never to instances
choices.why: The policy named `ec2:instance` in `enforced_for`; the resource type is the one it asked about.

choices.text: That the policy was attached to the wrong root
choices.why: An organisation has one root, and `list-roots` printed it before the policy was attached to it.

prompt: The `t3.medium` ran untagged from 1 to 14 October and was tagged `team=data` on the 15th. The key `team` was activated in September. Which part of its October cost appears under `team$data`?
hint: The key was ready; was the tag?

choices.text: All of October, because the key was active before the month began
choices.why: An active key splits the lines that carry it. The first fourteen days' lines carry no tag at all.

choices.text: All of October, once a backfill is requested for the month
choices.why: A backfill applies an activation to earlier months. It cannot add a tag the resource did not carry at the time.

choices.text: None of it until November, when the next bill is generated
choices.why: Lines are split as they are recorded, once the tag is on them; nobody waits for the next bill.

choices.text: From the 15th on; the first fourteen days stay under `team$`
choices.why: Right. The tag has to be on the resource when the cost happens. The days before it are the untagged remainder.

prompt: Put in order what happens between a new tag key and the first report that splits costs by it, as AWS's documentation describes it.
hint: Two waits of up to a day, one on each side of a person's click.
items: the key `team` is first used on a resource
the key appears in Billing's list of cost allocation tags
somebody in the management account activates it
reports split the new costs by `team`
trap: Putting the activation before the key appears in the list is the usual slip: Billing can only offer a key it has already seen on a resource.

prompt: Tag keys used to split the bill must be activated in Billing in the ___ account of the organisation.
hint: The account the consolidated bill belongs to.

prompt: `aws ce get-cost-and-usage` against moto answers `"ResultsByTime": []`. Why?
hint: What would moto add up?

choices.text: The key `team` has not been activated
choices.why: The query grouped by a dimension came back empty too. There is nothing to group.

choices.text: The period ends on the 1st, which excludes the whole month
choices.why: The end is exclusive, so `End=2026-10-01` is all of September. The period is right.

choices.text: moto bills nothing, so there is no spending to report
choices.why: Right. moto records resources and never charges them. The shape of the query is the lesson; the numbers would come from a real bill.

choices.text: Cost Explorer has to be enabled first, and preparing the data takes up to a day
choices.why: True of a real account the first time, but moto has no such step, and waiting would not fill the answer.

prompt: The data team paid 1,200 dollars upfront on 2 January for a year of capacity. Read with `UnblendedCost`, how does their year look?
hint: When is an upfront payment counted, unblended?

choices.text: A spike in the first month, then eleven months that look free
choices.why: Right. Unblended counts the charge on the day it was charged. Amortised would show 100 dollars in each month.

choices.text: 100 dollars in each of the twelve months, the payment spread evenly over the year
choices.why: That is `AmortizedCost`, which spreads an upfront payment over the hours it pays for.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since upfront payments are not usage
choices.why: The payment is a charge on the bill, and every metric counts it somewhere; they differ in when.

choices.text: The same as `NetUnblendedCost`, minus the 1,200
choices.why: Net subtracts discounts the account was given, not upfront payments.

prompt: Match each Cost Explorer metric to what it counts.
hint: Two differ in when; one in what is subtracted.

pairs.right: each charge on the day it was charged
upfront payments spread over the hours they cover
an average rate across a consolidated bill

prompt: A dashboard calls `get-cost-and-usage` every 5 minutes, all of a 30-day month. At the price list's 0.01 dollars per request, what does the month of requests cost?
hint: 12 an hour, 24 hours, 30 days.

prompt: A query reads `--time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-09-30 --granularity MONTHLY`. What does it miss?
hint: Is the end included?

choices.text: Nothing; September has thirty days
choices.why: It has, and the end date is exclusive, so the 30th is outside the period.

choices.text: The first day, because the start is exclusive
choices.why: The start is inclusive. It is the end that is left out.

choices.text: The month's tax, which MONTHLY granularity reports apart
choices.why: Granularity decides the size of each bucket of time, not which charges are counted.

choices.text: 30 September, silently
choices.why: Right. The end is exclusive, so the whole month is `End=2026-10-01`. Nothing warns that a day is missing.

prompt: Spending on NAT gateways triples one week, while the account's month stays under its budget. Which instrument is built to notice?
hint: One compares a total with a line; one compares a day with a pattern.

choices.text: The actual notification of the budget, at 80%
choices.why: The total is under the line, so the actual notification has nothing to fire on.

choices.text: A Cost Anomaly Detection monitor watching costs per service
choices.why: Right. It learns each service's usual pattern and reports a day that departs from it, whatever the total does.

choices.text: A Cost Explorer query grouped by `SERVICE`, which alerts on change
choices.why: It would show the change to somebody who asked. Cost Explorer answers questions; it sends no alert.

choices.text: A tag policy on the NAT gateways
choices.why: A tag policy governs how tags are spelt. It knows nothing about cost.

prompt: Finance asks how much the web team cost in September. The key `team` was activated on 20 September. What can an honest answer say?
hint: Activation is not retroactive by itself.

choices.text: The total under `team$web` for September, which is complete
choices.why: Before the 20th the key was not active, so those days' costs are not split by team at all.

choices.text: `team$web` from the 20th; the earlier days only after a backfill
choices.why: Right. A backfill applies the activation to earlier months, and it helps only where the resources already carried the tag.

choices.text: Nothing until October, the first whole month with the key
choices.why: The ten days after activation are split correctly; there is something to report, with its gap named.

choices.text: The September total divided by the number of teams
choices.why: That is an invention dressed as a number. Teams do not spend equally, and nothing in the bill says they did.

prompt: Match each question to the instrument of this lesson that answers it.
hint: Three instruments and one gate.

prompt: A staging account's GPU instance is left running over a weekend. The budget in the management account covers the whole organisation and has an actual notification at 80%. Why might nobody hear until Monday afternoon?
hint: Think about what the budget compares and how often.

choices.text: Budgets in the management account cannot see member accounts
choices.why: They see the whole consolidated bill; that is why the organisation's budget lives there.

choices.text: Alerts are held until the next working day, so a weekend is reported on Monday
choices.why: Nothing in AWS's documentation holds alerts for working days. The delay comes from refreshes and from the threshold.

choices.text: One account's spike is small against the whole total, and data refreshes a few times a day
choices.why: Right. A per-account budget, or an anomaly monitor per account, would have seen the staging spike on its own.

choices.text: A GPU instance is billed at the end of the month, not by the hour
choices.why: Instances are charged for the hours they run, and those hours reach the budget at each refresh.
